episode_thesis: Karniol-Tambour (Bridgewater) and Citrone (Discovery Capital) agree that the US-centred globalisation paradigm of the last 15 years is giving way to a more mercantilist, fragmented world that markets have barely begun to price, and that investors are over-concentrated in US assets. Both therefore favour taking risk mostly outside the US (Latin America and other EM for Citrone; non-US government bonds, euro and yen against the dollar, and broader asset-class flexibility for Karniol-Tambour), while differing on the US rates and growth path and on tactical oil versus gold (May 2025).

speakers.name: Karen Karniol-Tambour
speakers.role: Macro investor at Bridgewater (fundamental and systematic, global macro)
speakers.speaker_note: Captions have no speaker labels; the ledger infers her from content (secular-paradigm, Bridgewater-style systematic language). The opening question may come from Citrone or an unnamed moderator. The gold-versus-oil crowding argument at the end of C06 is probably Citrone's counterpoint (see ledger correction), so it is not credited to her here.

worldview_premises.premise: Investment returns over decades are driven by large secular paradigms. The last 15 years rested on globalisation, a US security umbrella and deflationary easy money, which made a plain S&P 500 the best asset.

A new paradigm of 'modern mercantilism' (state maximises national wealth and self-sufficiency, treats trade deficits as wealth transfers, treats allies coercively) is starting, and markets still price the old one.
worldview_premises.support: Argument that the shift predates Trump and runs through many countries; contrast with 2010 when US profitability was priced low and now it is priced high.

worldview_premises.premise: Reduced foreign appetite for US assets cannot unwind in a day because the trade deficit's flip side is large current-account inflows, mostly from allies, so adjustment is gradual.

Market-cap-guided investors are heavily concentrated in the US; real diversification needs markets with different growth, inflation, monetary policy and elections, and a portfolio that works under different economic outcomes.
worldview_premises.support: Argument from concentration; Mexico/Brazil tiny in world indices.

worldview_premises.premise: Tariffs are inflationary in the US (more so if they bring supply disruption) but deflationary abroad, so the Fed cannot easily ease while other central banks can.
worldview_premises.support: Comparison of the US with other countries' currency moves and energy prices; VAT-vs-Covid analogy for the Fed's dilemma.

worldview_premises.premise: Country views can be expressed in stocks, bonds and currencies, and doing so lets one earn from a country even when its stock market does badly; investors who express views only in equities forgo that range.
worldview_premises.support: China-only and ex-China funds were biggest winners; weak economy, good bonds, devalued currency.

worldview_premises.premise: Fixed income as a recession hedge was hollowed out in the zero-rate era as institutions moved to private credit, which carries equity-like risk; duration and cross-country currency selection are again sources of uncorrelated alpha.
Commodities, including gold, are ignored but useful assets in a world with more inflation risk.
worldview_premises.support: Argument that the long period without inflation made them look uninteresting.

worldview_premises.premise: US private-sector exceptionalism (technology, financial services, capital markets) persists, so capital will not leave the US easily, even as global investors begin to reduce their US overweight.
Countries are assessed like companies: management quality and policy come first; political change toward better management creates opportunity.
worldview_premises.support: Milei in Argentina and spreading regional change; four elections in 18 months.

worldview_premises.premise: The world is siloing into Americas, Europe and Asia blocs, which creates dislocations.
Because the world is tricky and dislocated, a portfolio needs shorts and dynamic protection rather than being structurally long.
Mexico and Brazil are negligible in market-cap terms (Nvidia fell by about two Mexicos on DeepSeek Monday), which shows how under-capitalised they are in world indices.
Rising US yields push yields higher in most other countries, so rates fall only where local conditions differ (Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Turkey).

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Speaker attribution is uncertain for C02-4 (two Mexicos story) and the gold-oil crowding sentence in C06; the ledger corrections reassign them to Citrone.
Karniol-Tambour says a systematic measure shows once-in-10-to-15-year pressure, but gives no metric, universe or threshold.
Citrone's 5-5.25% 10-year forecast and 2026 boom are given without a horizon beyond year-end 2025 or any sizing; Karniol-Tambour's yield view is not stated despite 'we differ a little'.
Oil is bought for a near-term spike but he is unsure long term; no exit rule.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Policy inputs: tariff announcements and de-escalation, US fiscal bill (tax cuts versus spending cuts), reshoring decisions, Fed communication on tariff inflation. Market inputs: positioning in gold and oil, the Treasury term/risk premium, speed of foreign allocation shifts away from the US, EM election outcomes (Peru, Colombia, Chile, Brazil), Brazil rate path. Horizon: months for rates and currency, through 2026 for the growth rebound and Brazil, years for the paradigm.
reader_inferences: (reader) The two disagree less on direction (outside-US tilt) than on the US cycle: Citrone expects a strong US 2026 with higher yields while Karniol-Tambour expects slowdown plus sticky inflation.
(reader) Both approaches avoid market-cap weighting; Citrone chooses by country management quality, Karniol-Tambour by diversification across growth, inflation and policy regimes.
(reader) Karniol-Tambour's non-US bond view and Citrone's short Japan bonds are compatible only if the stronger-yen/euro currency view dominates the rate view.
